title: How Uber uses AI for development: inside look
takeaways: Uber's AI tooling (Minion, Shepherd, uReview) with 84% dev adoption. Reporting was solid but not surprising — the more interesting question is whether companies use AI tools as learning accelerators vs shortcuts, and what that means for engineer quality over time.

title: The Shape of the Thing
takeaways: METR long task benchmark shows exponential growth in AI autonomous capability — y-axis measures task complexity by human-hours. The 'otters on wifi' image generation comparison powerfully illustrates exponential improvement that's hard to perceive in the moment. Sparked reflection on personal AI adoption progression (Copilot → ChatGPT → Cursor → autonomous agents) and where the value of learning programming languages sits now.

title: Slow is Fast: Why Rushing AI Adoption Backfires on Productivity
takeaways: Long tail of demand is the real insight — AI makes it viable to solve niche problems too small for vendors. Rate-determining step metaphor: org bottlenecks govern adoption speed, not AI capability. Weak on specifics — claims to fact-check viral AI claims but doesn't cite the actual stories (Klarna, IBM, Chegg). Prompted useful self-reflection on personal automation opportunities (Miro boarding, kickoff prep).

title: Migrating millions of lines of code to TypeScript
takeaways: Stripe migrated 3.7M lines from Flow to TypeScript in a single PR. Big-bang approach chosen because tight coupling made incremental migration impractical. A year of codemod preparation made the risky day boring. Shipped with 37,000 @ts-expect-error suppressions — pragmatism over perfectionism. Well-written but no explosive insights.

title: Retrieval After RAG: Hybrid Search, Agents, and Database Design — Simon Hørup Eskildsen of Turbopuffer
takeaways: Advancements in other technologies can trigger advancements in new ones — S3 strong consistency (2020), NVMe SSDs (2017), and compare-and-swap (2024) converged to enable a fundamentally different database architecture. When making design decisions, think of where they could potentially be disruptive. Founded on napkin math, not market research. Design philosophy: optimize for what won't wake you at 3 AM — no consensus layer, S3 as single source of truth, stateless servers.

title: What If the Best Time to Exercise Is Right After You Put Down Your Fork?
takeaways: Post-meal walking blunts blood sugar spikes (~17% reduction). Timing matters — immediate post-meal beats delayed. Pre-meal exercise doesn't blunt the spike but does help with overall glucose disposal via glycogen replenishment. Well-cited for a short health article but nothing new.

title: Why the ATM Didn't Kill Bank Tellers
takeaways: Task automation (ATMs) vs paradigm shifts (iPhones) have different labor effects. Extended to AI/engineers: demand only drops when bottleneck moves away from code. Real constraint isn't coding capability—it's gathering scattered context and resolving ambiguity in complex systems. LLMs can organize explicit information but cannot navigate, disambiguate, or understand implicit tradeoffs. Domain expertise becomes the binding constraint, not code generation.

title: Why I'm Not Worried About AI Job Loss
takeaways: Argues comparative advantage over absolute advantage: even if AI beats humans at everything, human+AI often outperforms either alone. Regulatory friction and organizational inertia persist as bottlenecks. Elastic demand will drive more work, not fewer jobs. Weakness: descriptive not prescriptive—shows a future but doesn't help prepare for it. Real preparation = manage AI agents well AND build deep domain expertise so you understand *why* decisions matter, not just *how* to code them.

title: How Organizations Lose Their Minds
takeaways: Four-stage organizational decline: information becomes fiction → quarterly pressure → leaders stop thinking → collapse. Blockbuster/Circuit City examples compelling. BUT: the AI layoff comparison overstates the case—those companies were in sunset/disrupted industries where structural headwinds made recovery hard. AI layoffs are different. Core insight remains valuable: short-termism and lost visibility are genuine failure modes. Importance of staying grounded: thinking, listening, and seeing—not rationalizing.
